planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall to cold-stratify over winter, or plant container stock in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; unlike vining clematis this species forms a non-climbing clump and needs no trellis.

directions: Sugarbowls is a non-climbing, herbaceous clematis of dry foothills, sagebrush flats, and prairie edges from the Rocky Mountains to the Great Plains, forming a low clump of finely divided, silvery-hairy foliage topped in spring with solitary, nodding, thick-petaled flowers in dull purple-brown, densely covered in fine hairs that give the upside-down, urn-shaped bloom its sugar-bowl silhouette. The flowers are followed by showy, silvery, feather-plumed seed heads that persist well into summer. Plant in lean, fast-draining, often rocky or sandy soil in full sun, where it is exceptionally drought-tolerant once established and resents soggy winter conditions; it needs no support or pruning beyond tidying spent foliage in fall.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, well-drained soil with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into sun; this cold-hardy East Asian species tolerates harsher winters than many ornamental clematis.

directions: Dusky virgin's bower is a twining climbing species from Siberia, the Russian Far East, Korea, and Japan, producing nodding, thick-textured bell-shaped flowers in dusky purple-brown densely clothed in rusty, velvety hairs, giving the whole bloom an unusually dark, furry appearance distinct from the typical flat clematis flower. It blooms in summer on a modest, twining vine that scrambles through a low fence, shrub, or trellis, followed by the fluffy silver seed heads typical of the genus. Being adapted to harsh continental winters, it is among the more cold-hardy climbing species in the genus and tolerates poor or rocky soil once established.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy support; like C. armandii this evergreen species blooms on the previous year's growth, so prune only right after flowering.

directions: Hooked clematis is a vigorous evergreen climbing species native to central and southern China and Taiwan, named for the hooked, clasping leaf stalks that help it grip a support as it scrambles upward. In spring it bears abundant clusters of small, fragrant, pure white star-shaped flowers set against glossy, leathery divided leaflets that hold their color through mild winters. It needs a sturdy fence, arbor, or tree to climb and performs best in the milder end of its hardiness range, pairing well with C. armandii or C. cirrhosa where an evergreen, fragrant clematis is wanted; keep the root zone cool and shaded while the vine reaches into full sun.

common_name: Alba Plena Florida Clematis (Historic Double White Floridatype Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with roots shaded and cool; this floridatype cultivar blooms on both old and new wood, so prune only lightly to shape and remove dead stems rather than cutting hard back.

directions: One of the oldest double-flowered clematis known in cultivation, Alba Plena produces fully double, rosette-form flowers in creamy white, the many narrow inner tepals sometimes faintly tinged green at the center, opening from late spring into summer on a comparatively compact, well-mannered vine. Because flowering occurs on both the previous year's ripened wood and new growth, it belongs to the light-pruning group of clematis — only tidy and shape it after the main flush rather than cutting the whole plant back hard. Give it a modest trellis or obelisk with roots shaded and cool while the vine reaches into full to partial sun.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with roots shaded and cool; prune lightly to shape since this floridatype cultivar flowers on both old and new wood.

directions: Pistachio is a modern double floridatype cultivar bearing an unusual two-tiered flower: flat, pale greenish-white outer tepals surround a dense, raised central cluster of smaller, purple-tipped green-and-white petals, giving each bloom an almost anemone-like, layered appearance unlike the typical open clematis flower. It blooms over a long season from late spring into summer on a compact vine well suited to a container or small obelisk. Because it flowers on both old and new growth, prune only lightly after the main spring flush to shape and remove dead wood, keeping roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full to partial sun.

common_name: Lady Northcliffe Clematis (Older Lavender-Blue Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into sun; this older large-flowered hybrid flowers on both old and new wood, so prune only lightly after the first flush.

directions: Lady Northcliffe is an older large-flowered hybrid clematis bearing soft lavender-blue, broad-petaled flowers with contrasting cream stamens, opening in a strong early-summer flush and continuing more sparsely into late summer. Like other early-to-midseason large-flowered types, it blooms on both the previous year's ripened stems and new growth, so pruning should be light — just removing dead or weak growth and shaping after the main display rather than cutting hard back. Give it a trellis or fence with roots kept cool and shaded while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade.

common_name: Fairy Queen Clematis (Blush Pink Large-Flowered Clematis with Carmine Bar)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into sun; prune only lightly since this older large-flowered hybrid blooms on both old and new wood.

directions: Fairy Queen is one of the older English large-flowered clematis hybrids, producing pale blush-pink flowers accented by a deeper carmine-pink central bar down each petal, most pronounced on the earliest flowers of the season. It flowers on both the previous year's growth and new wood in an early flush followed by a lighter repeat later in summer, so pruning should be limited to shaping and removing dead stems after the first flowering rather than cutting the whole plant back. Grow on a trellis or fence with the roots shaded and cool and the top growth in full sun to light shade.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into sun; prune only lightly since this cultivar's early double flowers form on old wood, with a later single or semi-double flush on new growth.

directions: Royalty bears fully double, rich lavender-blue flowers with a faintly silvery sheen in its early-season flush on the previous year's growth, followed by a lighter repeat of simpler, single or semi-double blooms on new growth later in the season. Its relatively compact size compared to older large-flowered hybrids makes it a good choice for a large container, obelisk, or small trellis near a patio. Keep roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade, and limit pruning to shaping and removing dead wood after the first flowering rather than cutting hard back.
